pr.title: bootstrap: add an rpath to libLLVM for the distributed `rust-objcopy`
pr.body:
Fixes rust-lang/rust#164063.

`rust-objcopy` is a renamed copy of `llvm-objcopy`, shipped in the `rustc` component at `lib/rustlib/$host/bin/`. When LLVM is linked dynamically, the copy keeps LLVM's default rpath, `$ORIGIN/../lib` (`@loader_path/../lib` on darwin). That resolves to `lib/rustlib/$host/lib/`, but the `rustc` component ships `libLLVM` only in `lib/`. So `rust-objcopy` fails to load unless rustup's `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`/`DYLD_FALLBACK_LIBRARY_PATH` override is in effect or the `llvm-tools` component is installed. rustc runs it to strip debuginfo, and it reports a failed strip only as a warning, so release binaries silently keep their debuginfo.

rust-lang/rust#163954 fixed the same problem for `rust-lld` in `Lld::run`. `rust-objcopy` is built by the `Llvm` step instead, so that fix doesn't reach it. This PR adds the same rpath entry, `$ORIGIN/../../../` on Linux and `@loader_path/../../../` on darwin, to the executable linker flags of the main LLVM build, behind the same `rpath_enabled`/`use_host_linker` guards. The extra entry only adds a search path for the other LLVM tools: in `llvm-tools`, those still resolve through `rustlib/$host/lib`.

Observed on 1.98.1 outside rustup's overrides:

- aarch64-apple-darwin: dyld aborts with `Library not loaded: @rpath/libLLVM.dylib` (SIGABRT). This is a regression since rust-lang/rust#157205.
- x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu: `libLLVM.so.22.1-rust-1.98.1-stable: cannot open shared object file`. The same `$ORIGIN/../lib`-only runpath is present back to at least 1.89.

### Testing

- `cargo check` of bootstrap and `rustfmt --check` pass.
- I validated the rpath value by hand on a copy of the 1.98.1 darwin toolchain layout. `rust-objcopy` exits with SIGABRT as shipped, and works after `install_name_tool -add_rpath @loader_path/../../../` and an ad-hoc re-sign.
- I have not run a full `./x dist` locally. Like rust-lang/rust#163954, there doesn't seem to be a dist test that covers this, so CI artifacts are the real check.

The `download-ci-llvm-stamp` is bumped because CI LLVM artifacts change.

cc @rami3l @sgasho

<sub>Disclosure: the diagnosis, patch and description were produced with an LLM (Claude). I reviewed them and checked the observations above on my own machines.</sub>

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

commits.messageBody:
`rust-objcopy` is a renamed copy of `llvm-objcopy` shipped in the `rustc`
component at `lib/rustlib/$host/bin`. When LLVM is linked dynamically it
only carries LLVM's default `$ORIGIN/../lib` (`@loader_path/../lib` on
darwin) rpath, which does not reach the `libLLVM` shipped in `lib/`, so it
fails to load outside rustup's library path overrides.

Mirror the rpath entry `Lld::run` already adds for `rust-lld` on the LLVM

pr.title: Use u64 limbs in core::num::bignum
pr.body:
## Summary

This PR changes `core::num::bignum` to use `u64` limbs instead of `u32` limbs.

This follows the unlocking of `u128` in rust-lang/rust#146277 and the related discussion in rust-lang/rust#137887, which noted that `core::num::bignum` should have a `u64` digit path.

The total capacity of the bignum remains unchanged at 1280 bits, while the number of limbs is reduced from 40 to 20.

## Changes

* Change `Digit32 = u32` / `Big32x40` to `Digit64 = u64` / `Big64x20`.
* Add the `u64` entry to `SMALL_POW5`.
* Update the `POW5` tables used by the `dragon` float-to-decimal conversion strategy to use 64-bit limbs.
* Update the corresponding `coretests` to use `Big64x20`.
* Adjust `from_u64` to avoid shifting by the type width when instantiated with `u64`:

  * replace `v >>= <$ty>::BITS` with `checked_shr(...).unwrap_or(0)`.
  * The previous expression triggers `arithmetic_overflow` when the macro is instantiated with `u64`, and shifting by the type width would not be valid at runtime either.

The `POW5` tables were regenerated from the corresponding powers of five and cross-checked against the existing 32-bit tables.

## Performance

I benchmarked the existing `Big32x40` implementation against the new `Big64x20` implementation under the same build profile and on the same machine.

| Benchmark               | Big32x40 (ns/iter) | Big64x20 (ns/iter) | Speedup |
| ----------------------- | -----------------: | -----------------: | ------: |
| `bench_big_exact_inf`   |             33,568 |            ~21,700 |   1.55x |
| `bench_big_shortest`    |              2,913 |             ~1,880 |   1.55x |
| `bench_big_exact_12`    |              1,680 |             ~1,030 |   1.63x |
| `bench_big_exact_3`     |                878 |               ~585 |   1.50x |
| `bench_small_exact_inf` |              1,353 |             ~1,425 |   ~1.0x |
| `bench_small_exact_12`  |                277 |               ~220 |   1.26x |
| `bench_small_exact_3`   |                170 |               ~134 |   1.27x |
| `bench_small_shortest`  |                320 |               ~275 |   1.16x |

The larger inputs, where the bignum uses many limbs, show roughly a 1.5–1.6x speedup. Smaller inputs show a more modest improvement, while `bench_small_exact_inf` is effectively unchanged within measurement noise.

These are local measurements; the rust-timer results on the PR should provide the authoritative benchmark comparison.

## Testing

The following tests pass locally:

```text
./x test library/coretests --test-args bignum
./x test library/coretests --test-args flt2dec
./x test tidy
```

## Notes

This change applies the `u64` limb representation to all targets; there is currently no target-specific conditional compilation to retain the `u32` representation on 32-bit targets.

On 32-bit targets, using `u64` limbs may have a higher arithmetic cost because 64-bit operations can require multiple instructions. However, the affected `dragon` implementation is a fallback path rather than a common hot path.

The total bignum size remains unchanged at 1280 bits (160 bytes), since 20 `u64` limbs occupy the same amount of storage as 40 `u32` limbs.

If maintaining a `u32` instantiation for 32-bit targets is preferred, I would be happy to follow up with a target-specific implementation.

Fixes rust-lang/rust#137887

pr.title: Add an AGENTS.md that enforces the LLM policy
pr.body:
<!-- homu-ignore:start -->
*[View all comments](https://triagebot.infra.rust-lang.org/gh-comments/rust-lang/rust/pull/160997)*
<!-- homu-ignore:end -->

The goal here is to *reduce the amount of slop PRs*, not as a blanket endorsement of using agents to work on `rust-lang/rust`.
For more info about motivation, see [the blog post](https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/08/05/rust-langrust-is-adopting-an-llm-policy/).

To that end, I have [done extensive testing][ETOOMANYLUNAS] to make sure the new file actually helps that goal.
The results are promising.
They show agents consistently asking their users to confirm they're read their own work;
requiring users to write their own PR descriptions;
and pointing people to other repos if they try to modify a submodule or subtrees,
as well as various other tests.

[ETOOMANYLUNAS]: https://github.com/jyn514/ETOOMANYLUNAS

Almost all of the AGENTS.md was itself generated with an LLM.
See the [linked testing repo][ETOOMANYLUNAS] for more information about testing and methodology.
I wrote this PR description and both commit descriptions myself.

---

Summary of the AGENTS.md (taken from the test repo):

This is a rather long operationalization of the [dev-guide] as algorithmic instructions.
Most of it was itself generated with an agent.

Differences between this and the [dev-guide] / [policy]:

[dev-guide]: https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/llm-guidance.html
[policy]: https://forge.rust-lang.org/policies/llm-usage.html

- "strong suggestions" in the docs are turned into absolute requirements here; LLMs have trouble with discretion and judgement.
- lang/edition/etc are not exempted; determining what falls under their scope was too hard to operationalize. members of those teams can still write their own AGENTS.md if this one interferes with their work (i wouldn’t expect it to, though, it’s mostly focused on code.)
- the LLM requires a reviewer before making edits, not before posting the PR. experimental PRs are not exempted (how could the LLM know it was experimental?).
- soundness changes are always rejected, even if allowed by the policy (how could the LLM know you’re in the org?)

This is not exhaustive; if you want a more detailed human-facing summary, see the [dev-guide].

---

The second commit adds a CLAUDE.md that links directly to AGENTS.md.
This adds one vendor-specific file, for the benefit of getting Claude to
actually follow the instructions.

I've put this in a separate commit so that I can drop it if people feel
strongly. I *highly recommend* that we add a CLAUDE.md, it really makes
a difference. You can see examples of what Claude does without a file in
the [testing repo][ETOOMANYLUNAS].

[ETOOMANYLUNAS]: https://github.com/jyn514/ETOOMANYLUNAS
